Q-IP-01.text: Have you recorded why this type of model suits your problem and data?
Q-IP-01.expectedPractice: You record the model types you considered, why the chosen one fits the problem, the data and the people who must understand or maintain it, and what you gave up by choosing it.
Q-IP-01.whyAsked: A model chosen by habit can be harder to explain and maintain than the problem needs; a written choice tells later users what it is for.
evidenceExamples: the model choice note
the methods section of the protocol
a comparison table of candidate models

answerLabels.partly: Partly, some of it is recorded
answerLabels.not_applicable: A choice of model does not apply

answerPrompts.not_yet: Name the model type you expect and when you will record the choice; it prints in the model card.
answerPrompts.not_applicable: Say why no choice of model type applies; it prints in the model card.

Q-IP-02.text: Have you checked that your training, validation and test sets come from the same population?
Q-IP-02.expectedPractice: You split the data into training, validation and test sets so no person, household or site is in more than one where that would leak information, check they come from the same population, and record how the test set differs from the setting of use.
Q-IP-02.whyAsked: Test data that overlaps the training data, or comes from another population, makes reported performance wrong in ways nobody sees until the system is in use.
evidenceExamples: the data split code or its description
a table comparing the sets by group and source
the evaluation section of the protocol

answerLabels.not_applicable: Splitting the data does not apply

Q-IP-03.text: Have you measured the kinds of error your model makes, for example with a confusion matrix, precision, recall, specificity and F1?
Q-IP-03.expectedPractice: On held-out test data, you report the confusion matrix and the measures that matter for your use, such as precision, recall, specificity and F1, and record which error costs the people affected more, and so which measure you watch most.
Q-IP-03.whyAsked: Accuracy alone can hide a model that misses most cases that matter, and whether a missed case or a false alarm is worse depends on the use.
evidenceExamples: the evaluation report with the confusion matrix
the summary file from the evaluation notebook
a link to the metrics in the repository

answerLabels.not_applicable: Measuring errors does not apply

answerPrompts.not_yet: Say when you will measure the errors on held-out data, or what is blocking it.

Q-IP-04.text: Have you measured performance separately for each relevant group, for example by age, gender or ethnicity?

Each result gives its number of cases, and you name groups too small for a reliable estimate rather than leave them out.
Q-IP-04.whyAsked: A model can look good on average and still work badly for one group, whose people carry the cost of its errors.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-14 notebook
a per-group metrics table with group sizes

Q-IP-06.text: Which fairness measures have you computed?
Q-IP-06.expectedPractice: You choose the fairness measures that fit how your system's errors affect people, compute them for the groups you compare and record why those. Most systems that predict something about people need an error-rate measure and a calibration or precision measure. You explain each unticked measure as not fitting and name any fitting measure not listed.
Q-IP-06.whyAsked: Fairness measures answer different questions and cannot all hold at once, so a result means something only if the measures fit the use and you say why.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the C-13 notebook
a fairness report with the measures by group
the decision note on which measures fit

Q-IP-08.text: Have you tested the model on data unlike its training data, such as noisy, incomplete or unusual inputs?
Q-IP-08.expectedPractice: You test the model on inputs that differ from its training data in the ways expected in use, such as added noise, missing or wrong values, rare cases, lower image or sound quality, and other dialects, devices or sites, with methods such as perturbation tests, held-out sites or the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox. You record how much performance changed and what you did.
Q-IP-08.whyAsked: Field data is noisier than training data, so a model never tested on worse inputs can lose much of its accuracy in use without warning.
evidenceExamples: the summary file from the perturbation part of the C-18 notebook
a robustness test report
results on a held-out site or device
